questions.text: How many years until you expect to need a large part of this money?
questions.help: The longer you can leave the money invested, the more time it has to recover from bad years. Give your best estimate, between 1 and 40 years.
If your income is steady, you are less likely to be forced to sell investments at a bad moment to pay your bills.

options.label: Very stable (permanent job, pension, civil service)
Uncertain, or likely to drop soon

questions.text: What share of all your savings and assets will this investment be?
questions.help: Count everything you own: savings, property, other investments. The bigger this investment is compared with the rest, the more a loss would hurt your overall situation.

questions.text: If your income stopped, how long could you cover your living costs from savings outside this investment?
questions.help: An emergency buffer in cash means you will not have to sell investments in a downturn just to get by. Experts often suggest three to six months of expenses.

questions.text: How likely is it that you will need to take money out before your planned horizon?
questions.help: Money you may need soon should not take big risks. Money you will not touch for many years can ride out the ups and downs.

options.label: Very unlikely, I will leave it untouched
Possible, if something unexpected comes up
Likely, I expect to withdraw soon or regularly

questions.text: Imagine your portfolio falls 20% within three months. What would you most likely do?
questions.help: Falls of 20% or more happen in markets from time to time. What matters is how you would really behave, because selling after a fall turns a temporary loss into a permanent one.

options.label: Sell everything to stop the losses
Sell part of it to feel safer
Do nothing and wait for a recovery
Invest more while prices are low

questions.text: Which range of possible results over one year would you choose?
questions.help: Higher possible gains usually come with bigger possible losses. There is no right answer, pick the range you would be most comfortable living with.

questions.text: How much experience do you have with investing in stocks, funds or ETFs?
questions.help: Experience through good and bad markets usually shows how you react to a fall. If you are new to investing, that is fine, we simply take a more careful starting point.

options.label: None, this is my first time
A little, for less than 3 years

questions.text: Which sentence describes you best as an investor?
questions.help: Your own gut feeling about risk is a useful signal. It is combined with the more factual answers, and you can adjust the final result yourself.

options.label: I want safety, even if returns are low
I prefer stability with a little growth
I accept some ups and downs for better returns
I accept big swings for the highest long-term returns

questions.text: What is the largest loss over one year that you could accept without losing sleep?
questions.help: Picture this as a share of your whole investment: a 20% loss on 10,000 is 2,000. Choose the largest loss you could truly live with.

options.label: None, I want to keep my money safe
